text:
Date: 19991021

Docket: D109829

Registry: Vancouver

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

GAIL MAMMON a.k.a. GAIL LIPKOWITZ

PETITIONER

AND:

NORMAN NATHAN MAMMON

RESPONDENT

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE MR.
JUSTICE LOWRY

The
Petitioner:

In person

The
Respondent:

In person

Place and
Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

October 15, 1999

[
1
]

Norman Mammon and
Gail Lipkowitz were married in 1990.  When they separated in 1997, they entered
into an agreement with respect to their two young children, Benjamin and
Rebecca, now aged seven and four respectively.  It provides for joint custody
and guardianship with the children's principle residence being with their
mother.  Frequent, stipulated access is afforded to their father who is to pay
$800 a month for their support.  It is agreed that neither will take the
children out of the jurisdiction without the consent of the other or a court
order.  Ms. Lipkowitz wishes to take the children to live in Toronto and applies
for an order permitting her to do so.  The question, as in all matters of this
kind, is whether that will be in the children’s best interest.

[
2
]

Ms. Lipkowitz
applies for a decree of divorce, an order awarding her sole custody and
guardianship of the children, and permission to move out of the province.  Mr.
Mammon raises no objection to the divorce and I am satisfied a decree should be
granted.  However, he strongly opposes the balance of the application.

[
3
]

The many affidavits
filed show Mr. Mammon and Ms. Lipkowitz to be committed, loving parents.  The
children attend Jewish private school and are well cared for whether they are
with their mother or their father.  They have the benefit of extended family on
both sides.  Ms. Lipkowitz maintains a comfortable three bedroom home in the
west end of Vancouver.  She works as an operating room nurse four days a week
and employs a babysitter who has been with the children now for some time.  Mr.
Mammon lives in his parents’ home.  He is an investment adviser.  He has the
children with him every Wednesday in the late afternoon and evening and every
weekend from noon on Saturday to noon on Sunday, all as provided by the
agreement.  When they are with their father, the children enjoy regular contact
with what appears to be a large, close-knit family.

[
4
]

Ms. Lipkowitz wants
to move to Toronto with the children to be close to her parents as well as to
her brother, his wife, and their young children.  She maintains that her
employment opportunities would be enhanced and she believes her cost of living
would be less.  But she says she would not be seeking to make such a move if
Mr. Mammon was doing his part by cooperating with her in the care of the
children.  In this regard she has two complaints.

[
5
]

She first says, and
the fact is, that Mr. Mammon has not paid the child support he agreed to pay.
Early in 1998 he offered to pay half the amount agreed.  When Ms. Lipkowitz
refused he stopped making any payments and applied for an order fixing his
support for the children at what he contended would be in accordance with the
Federal Child Support Guidelines.  His application was unsuccessful.  An appeal
is pending.  Ms. Lipkowitz was forced to seek the assistance of the Family
Maintenance Enforcement Program.  Mr. Mammon  has not earned much money for
many months and Ms. Lipkowitz has received only relatively small amounts
garnisheed from his income.  The arrears now exceed $12,000.  Ms. Lipkowitz has
been forced to rely on financial contributions from her family to maintain her home.
Her father makes mortgage payments of $600 a month.  She struggles to cover the
considerable cost of the children’s school and does what she can to make ends
meet.

[
6
]

Ms. Lipkowitz then
says that Mr. Mammon will not communicate with her in any acceptable manner
regarding the children.  She says that the whole of her life is consumed by
working and caring for the children such that she has no time left to herself,
nor time to get on with making a new life.  As I understand her, Ms. Lipkowitz
says that, despite her repeated requests, Mr. Mammon will not commit to caring
for the children at any time other than the stipulated access periods.  While
in the first affidavit she filed, she says that there is no communication
between herself and Mr. Mammon, in the second she says that he harasses and
threatens her on a daily basis and does anything he can to make the situation
difficult.  For his part, Mr. Mammon says that he has been trying for some time
to arrange additional access for one complete weekend a month, for which the
agreement provides, but Ms. Lipkowitz seldom answers his calls and will not
discuss it with him.

[
7
]

To my observation,
based on their appearance before me, the relationship between Ms. Lipkowitz and
Mr. Mammon has deteriorated to the point where they appear incapable of
communicating beyond idle accusation and bickering.  At present the animosity
between them would appear to render sharing the responsibilities of custody, if
not guardianship, all but impossible.  Certainly Mr. Mammon’s refusal to pay
support in the face of an order of this court would appear to be at the heart
of much of the difficulty with which Ms. Lipkowitz finds herself confronted.
It is hard to reconcile his professed commitment to the welfare of his children
with his failure to make even one voluntary payment for their support for more
than a year and a half.  In the circumstances, his assertion that he will do
anything he can to ensure they continue to live in Vancouver rings somewhat
hollow, although he says that he now intends to resume making support payments
to Ms. Lipkowitz.

[
8
]

However, what
appears to me to be lacking in Ms. Lipkowitz’s application with respect to
moving to Toronto is any sound basis upon which it can be said that the move
would be in the children’s best interest when they would be deprived of the
continued close involvement they have with their father and his family.  Ms.
Lipkowitz insists that she has no desire to do anything to impair the
children’s relationship with their father, but, in advocating the move for the
reasons she gives, she seems to discount entirely the value of the time they
spend with him, and the extent to which he is a part of their everyday life.
These are very young children who have had to cope with their parents’
separation.  Must they now be told they are to be taken from their home,
friends, and family in this city and moved across the country with the prospect
of returning only for periods of vacation?

[
9
]

This is not a case
where a custodial parent has compelling reasons to make a substantial
geographical move (
see
Levesque v.
Lapointe

(1993),
1993 CanLII 1535 (BC CA)
,
44
R.F.L. (3d) 316 (B.C.C.A.)
).  In my view, it is rather a case where, one parent
who once recognized the importance of both parents continuing to play an active
role in the raising of their children after separation, as evidenced by the
agreement that was made, seeks to move to enable her to obtain assistance in
caring for the children, not because their present care is in any way
inadequate, but because she wants more time to herself to enable her to rebuild
her own life.

[
10
]

The circumstances
here are somewhat similar to those
in
Harrison v. Harrison

(1994),
1994 CanLII 1465 (BC SC)
,
2 B.C.L.R. (3d) 293 (S.C.)
.  There, following a
separation, a mother who was endeavouring to build a new life was going to move
with her children to live closer to a man with whom she had developed a
relationship.  Previously, the parties had consented to an order that the
children would live in close proximity to their father who shared joint
custody.  On the father’s application, the mother was restrained from moving
because it was not in the children’s best interest to separate them from him
given that he played a very active care-giving role in their lives.

[
11
]

Ms. Lipkowitz’s
frustration over her situation is certainly understandable, but it does not
justify a move that would impair the children’s life with their father to the
extent that would result from a move to Toronto.  Such a move would not be in
their best interest.

[
12
]

It follows that Ms.
Lipkowitz’s application to take the children out of the jurisdiction is to be
dismissed, but her application for sole custody and guardianship remains.  As
indicated, the present level of animosity between the parties renders them
unsuited to a regime of shared responsibilities.  Certainly, joint custody is
only workable where there is a reasonable level of responsible communication –
where separated parents are both willing and able to put the interests of their
children above any hostile feelings they may harbour.

[
13
]

I propose to adjourn
Ms. Lipkowitz’s application for sole custody and guardianship generally with
directions that it not be brought on again for at least six months.  It may be
that with the current issue of the move to Toronto behind them, and Mr. Mammon
having the opportunity to address the issue of support, the circumstances will
be different.  The relationship may be sufficiently improved to render the
sharing of the responsibilities inherent in custody and guardianship workable.
If not, it will be open to Ms. Lipkowitz to seek a disposition of her
application and I will consider myself seized of that matter.

[
14
]

There will then be a
decree of divorce.  The application for sole custody and guardianship is
adjourned generally with direction that it not be further heard for at least
six months.  The application for permission to take the children out of the
jurisdiction is dismissed.

"Lowry J."
